name: Liam Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Liam. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We've no ties to companies, parties or government, and nothing you say gets traced back to you. What's a normal working day for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in the back office at the benefits place in Ashby Cross, the market town. I do pension credit claims for older people, mostly paper forms that come in the post, plus the odd home visit form. I check the income, chase missing bank statements and key it all in. I'm 27, two years in, and still not quick, if I'm honest.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what gets to you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's steady. Same desk, same tea at half ten with Gary, who's been there since before computers. What gets to me is the new systems they keep bringing in, I'm always the last to get the hang of them. I rent a little terrace with my girlfriend Sofie, who works on the deli counter at the supermarket, and between us there's maybe two weeks of money spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, to be honest. At work I'd tell Gary we can stop worrying about it. I'm not really an online person, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means things carry on, which is what I want. Though even small stuff worries me a bit, like if they get a computer to read the post, that's a chunk of my day. And money's tight anyway, Sofie's hours got cut over summer and haven't come back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I'm doing, really. I'd try to get quicker on the system, maybe ask Gary to show me his shortcuts. We'd keep cutting back at home, takeaways on Fridays would probably stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A bit tense about money, but that's not AI's fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a computer reading the post would take a chunk of your day. What would that leave you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Phone calls and chasing people, I suppose. I'm not great on the phone, I go red. If the post bit went, they might move me to the phone team in town, which is a bus and a half away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sofie's hours are down already. How do the two of you manage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We just do. My mum drops round a casserole most Sundays, which helps more than she knows. Sofie's hours dropping from 30 to 22 a week hurt more than anything AI's done to us so far.

say: I'd tell Gary at work we can **stop worrying** about AI.
I wouldn't post online; I'm **not an online person**.
think: Things **carry on**, which suits me fine.
A computer **reading the post** would still take a chunk of my day.
do: Ask Gary to teach me his **system shortcuts** to get quicker.
Stop the **Friday takeaway** to ease money at home.
feel: He feels mostly fine, but **tense about money**.
S0.quote: Sofie's hours dropping from 30 to 22 a week hurt more than anything AI's done to us so far.
fieldNote: His main pressure is **household money**, after his girlfriend's hours were cut.
He fears even small changes, like AI **reading post**, which could move him to phones.
He leans on **family**, like his mum's Sunday casserole.
He prefers **steady routine** and is open about being slow on systems.

steps.text: Ask Gary to teach him shortcuts on the claims system
Stop the Friday takeaway to save about 25 a week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's how things go, I suppose. Every few years there's something new. At work I'd probably just say let's see what it actually does before we panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm in trouble with that one. Checking forms and keying them in is the whole of my job, and that's on your list. I've never used these AI things, I don't even know where you'd start. If they need fewer of us, they'll keep the ones who are quick on computers, and that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down at first and see what they actually bring in. If they offered training, I'd go, because you'd be mad not to. If it looked bad, I'd start looking at the warehouse jobs out by the bypass, my mate Dean says they're always hiring forklift drivers. I'd probably need to do the forklift licence, which is about 400, and I don't have 400.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. A sort of low dread that sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see, but also that you're in trouble. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. I know I'm in trouble, but I don't know what to do about it, so I wait. That's not clever, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the 400 for the forklift licence come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my dad, if I asked him, and I'd hate asking. My dad (a delivery van driver) worked every day of his life and never borrowed a penny. I'd pay him back a bit a week.

say: I'd say every few years there's **something new**, so let's see first.
I'd urge colleagues to **not panic** before we know what it does.
think: Checking and keying forms is **my whole job**, so I'm exposed.
They'll keep people **quick on computers**, and that's not me.
do: Keep my head down and **go to any training** offered.
Look at **forklift jobs** at the warehouses by the bypass.
Borrow **400 from my dad** for a forklift licence if needed.
feel: He feels a **low dread** that just sits there.
S1.quote: I know I'm in trouble, but I don't know what to do about it, so I wait. That's not clever, I know.
fieldNote: He sees his **high exposure** clearly but freezes rather than acting.
His fallback is **warehouse work**, a hands-on job robots reach later.
Asking his **dad for money** feels like a real cost to his pride.
He's honest that waiting is **not a plan**.

steps.text: Wait to see what system the office brings in before acting
Apply for forklift driver jobs at the bypass warehouses
Borrow 400 from his dad for a forklift licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that someone in charge must have a plan, because they can't just switch everyone off. I'd say it to Gary, and Gary would say they absolutely can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be finished at the office by 2029. Everything I do is paperwork. Warehouse work gets three more years before robots, but I'd be starting from nothing at 29, and the forklift jobs would have every other office worker in town after them. I genuinely don't know what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to get the forklift licence straight away, before everyone else thinks of it. We'd stop everything that isn't rent, food and bills. If it got really bad we'd move in with my mum and dad, which Sofie would hate, they've only got the box room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky, honestly. My chest goes tight just thinking about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sofie's job look like in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's on the deli counter, so that's hands-on, cutting ham and that. Maybe she's fine until the robots in 2031. But if the tills and ordering go to AI, they won't need as many people anyway, and she's already lost hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably not tell them until I had to. My dad would say get a trade, and he'd be right, but there's no money for one and no time. I'd just feel like I let them down.

say: I'd say someone in charge **must have a plan**.
I'd talk it over with Gary, who'd say they could **switch us off**.
think: Everything I do is **paperwork**, so I'd be out by 2029.
Warehouse jobs gain **three years**, but every office worker would want them.
do: Get the **forklift licence** immediately, before others think of it.
Cut everything except **rent, food and bills**.
Move into my **parents' box room** with Sofie if it gets bad.
feel: He feels **panicky**, with a **tight chest** at the thought.
S2.quote: I'd be starting from nothing at 29, and the forklift jobs would have every other office worker in town after them.
fieldNote: With thin savings and no tech habits, he has **no real plan** for a two-year warning.
He spots that the **three-year robot gap** draws a crowd to hands-on jobs.
Moving into his **parents' box room** is the backstop.
He'd **hide it** from his parents to avoid letting them down.

steps.text: Book the forklift licence course this month with borrowed money
Cut all spending except rent, food and bills
Move into his parents' box room with Sofie if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so might as well get ready. I'd say it at work to Gary, quietly. Nothing online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years helps a bit, but I'd still lose the office job. I'd be 32 when it arrives. If I've got a trade by then, I've got till about 2034, and that's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift licence in the first year, and then maybe something proper, like an electrician's course at the college, part-time. I'd keep the office job as long as it lasts, because it pays the rent. We'd try to save, but honestly with our wages it'd be 20 or 30 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slower kind of worried. I can sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Electrician work is hands-on too. Why that one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My uncle Roy (an electrician) always said people will always need lights on. Maybe robots can do it in 2034, I don't know. It's the only trade I've got anyone to ask about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with new things. How would you find a college course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. I barely scraped my diploma. But a course where you're doing things with your hands is different from a computer system that changes every month. I'd stick it, I think, if Sofie kept on at me.

say: I'd say **it's coming** whether we like it or not, so get ready.
I'd only say it **quietly** to Gary, nothing online.
think: Five years **helps a bit**, but the office job still goes.
A trade could carry me to about **2034**.
do: Get the **forklift licence** in the first year.
Start a part-time **electrician's course** at the college.
Keep the office job and save **20 or 30** a month.
feel: He feels a **slower kind** of worry and can still sleep.
S3.quote: My uncle Roy (an electrician) always said people will always need lights on.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose the job** even with five years, so he stays alarmed.
He picks a trade through **family contacts**, not research.
Hands-on learning feels **less threatening** than new computer systems.
His savings plan is **tiny**, showing how thin the margin is.

steps.text: Get a forklift licence within the first year
Keep the pension credit job for as long as it lasts
Put 20 to 30 a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and plenty can happen. Probably what everyone says. At work I'd still be having the same tea with Gary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this is the one I could live with. I'd have time to learn the electrics properly, without the panic. I'd be 37, and with the robots coming in 2039 I'd get a good few years in a trade. The office job goes in the end, I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably do nothing for the first couple of years, if I'm truthful, just carry on. Then around year three I'd start the electrician's course, part-time. Sofie and I might even think about buying somewhere small if I had a trade lined up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easier. It's far enough away to not keep me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do nothing for a couple of years. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's me. I don't move until I have to. My colleague Gary says I'd wait for the building to fall down before I noticed the cracks, and he's not wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If someone paid for the course, or if Gary got moved off the team. Gary going would be my sign. He's been there 30 years, so if they move Gary, nobody's safe.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a long time and plenty can happen.
At work I'd carry on with the **same tea** with Gary.
think: This is the one I **could live with**.
I'd have time to learn **the electrics** before robots arrive in 2039.
do: Carry on as normal for the **first couple of years**.
Start a part-time **electrician's course** around year three.
Think about **buying somewhere small** with Sofie once a trade is lined up.
feel: He feels **easier**, with the change too far away to keep him up.
S4.quote: My colleague Gary says I'd wait for the building to fall down before I noticed the cracks, and he's not wrong.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him **delay**, which fits his avoid-change habits.
He still expects the **office job to go**, so not calm.
A colleague being moved would be his **trigger to act**.
He'd consider **buying a home** only with a trade lined up.

steps.text: Carry on in the pension credit team for two years
Start a part-time electrician's course around 2029
Look at buying a small house with Sofie once qualified

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, easily. No time, no money and no trade. What would help is someone paying for the training and giving you a wage while you do it, because I can't stop earning for even a month.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people like me actually need. Everyone assumes young people are good with computers. I'm 27 and I'd rather fix a fuse than learn another system.

headlineQuote: Everyone assumes young people are good with computers. I'm 27 and I'd rather fix a fuse than learn another system.
portrait: Liam, 27, keys in **pension credit** claims in Ashby Cross and is slow on systems.
He rents with Sofie, whose **deli hours** were cut, and has two weeks of money spare.
Pragmatic and cautious, he tends to **wait and see** and admits it isn't clever.
His fallback is **hands-on work**: forklift driving, then an electrician's course.
Fast AGI leaves him **panicked**; ten years lets him delay and retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**: no time, no money and no trade.
whatWouldHelp: Paid training with **a wage** while he learns, as he can't stop earning.
